High-level concepts for tuning a CrowdStrike Falcon prevention policy (concepts only, vendor-agnostic):

- Define policy objectives that balance protection with acceptable false positives; align decisions with risk tolerance and asset criticality. (unverified web source https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0474)
- Map detections to a recognized framework to guide rule prioritization and ensure coverage of attacker behaviors. (unverified web source https://attack.mitre.org/analytics)
- Establish a telemetry baseline: collect normal activity patterns for hosts, users, and software to distinguish benign activity from malicious actions. (unverified web source https://documentation.wazuh.com/current/user-manual/ruleset/mitre.html)
- Use analytics-driven tuning to reduce alert noise: calibrate thresholds, correlation windows, and suppression rules based on observed data, not guesses. (unverified web source https://attack.mitre.org/analytics)
- Roll out changes in stages (pilot group or monitor-only mode) to evaluate false positives, coverage, and performance before broader deployment. (unverified web source https://attack.mitre.org/analytics)
- Maintain explicit suppression and exclusions with clear change control and documentation; review regularly to prevent scope creep. (unverified web source https://documentation.wazuh.com/current/user-manual/ruleset/mitre.html)
- Validate changes through controlled testing (red team blue team exercises, synthetic activity) and track metrics such as alert rate, coverage of critical techniques, and mean time to respond. (unverified web source https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0474)
- Establish a cadence for policy reviews and updates, including stakeholder sign-off and a public changelog.

Note: These are high-level, non-implementation details intended for policy discussion and planning. For vendor-specific steps, consult CrowdStrike Falcon documentation and your security governance policies.

Concepts and detection logic for password spraying in Microsoft Sentinel (high-level, non-operational):
- Pattern to look for: many failed sign-ins across a large number of distinct accounts from the same source within a short time window. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/alert-classification-password-spray-attack)
- Data sources to leverage: sign-in related events (e.g., SignInLogs or Identity-related events) that include user/account, source IP, timestamp, and result/status of the logon attempt. Use these signals to identify cross-account failure patterns. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/alert-classification-password-spray-attack)
- Detection approach (high-level): perform time-binned aggregation by source (IP or host) and by accounts, counting failed attempts and counting distinct accounts within a window (e.g., 15–60 minutes). Trigger when both the volume of failures and the number of distinct targets exceed defined thresholds. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/alert-classification-password-spray-attack)
- Distinguishing factors: correlate with geography, device context, and risk signals to reduce false positives; prioritize signals that show breadth across many accounts rather than repeated failures on a single account. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/alert-classification-password-spray-attack)
- KQL-level concept (high-level): build a query that filters for failed sign-ins, groups by SourceIP and Account within a rolling window, computes counts of failed attempts and distinct accounts, and flags when thresholds are exceeded. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/alert-classification-password-spray-attack)

References to example implementations or discussion can be found in the following sources: unverified web source(s):
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/alert-classification-password-spray-attack
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/907993/kql-suggest-logic-for-netiq-use-cases

High-level concepts for BGP neighbours on Junos OS (conceptual, not step-by-step):

- BGP adjacency is formed between a local router and a peer by agreeing on session parameters (address, remote AS, and session state). This results in a BGP session that transitions through states (Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, Established). (unverified web source https://gist.github.com/chmutoff/5a1e8a04d694089acbc00b1565e953fa)

- Neighbours can be iBGP (same AS) or eBGP (different AS). The choice affects how next-hop attributes are propagated and how the session is established and maintained. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/expressroute/expressroute-config-samples-routing)

- In Junos, BGP sessions are organized in groups for scalability; each neighbour (or group of neighbours) participates in a specific address-family (e.g., IPv4 unicast). Grouping helps manage large topologies and policy application. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/expressroute/expressroute-config-samples-routing)

- Important session considerations include: matching remote AS, reachability to the neighbour IP, and is done with mechanisms like update-source when the BGP peer is reachable via a non-direct interface; eBGP sessions often require TTL considerations and may use authentication (MD5) and hold timers. (unverified web source https://gist.github.com/chmutoff/5a1e8a04d694089acbc00b1565e953fa; unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/expressroute/expressroute-config-samples-routing)

- Detection and troubleshooting (conceptual): monitor BGP session state transitions and look for a fall to Idle/Connect or failure to establish. Common causes include IP reachability issues, AS mismatches, update-source misconfigurations, authentication failures, or path/neighbor reachability problems. Once Established, verify that routes are being exchanged as expected and that next-hop reachability and policy filters are not inadvertently preventing advertisement. (unverified web source https://gist.github.com/chmutoff/5a1e8a04d694089acbc00b1565e953fa; unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/expressroute/expressroute-config-samples-routing)

- Practical takeaway: use a scalable grouping approach, keep iBGP full-mesh considerations in mind, ensure address-family alignment, and monitor session state and advertisements to detect misconfigurations early. (unverified web source https://gist.github.com/chmutoff/5a1e8a04d694089acbc00b1565e953fa; unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/expressroute/expressroute-config-samples-routing)

output_text: The CVSS v4.0 base score measures the vulnerability’s intrinsic severity—the severity of the vulnerability itself independent of any specific environment or timing factors (unverified web source (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln-metrics/cvss)). It is computed from eight base metrics, grouped into Exploitability (Attack Vector, Attack Complexity, Privileges Required, User Interaction) and Impact (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) (unverified web source (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2022/NIST.IR.8409.pdf)). The base score is a numerical value from 0.0 to 10.0 and is also represented as a vector string (unverified web source (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2022/NIST.IR.8409.pdf)). Temporal and Environmental metrics can modify the overall severity, but they are separate from the base score (unverified web source (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln-metrics/cvss)). In CVSS v4.0, there are changes to how some dimensions are represented, focusing on the core Exploitability and Impact metrics rather than a separate Scope metric (unverified web source (https://csrc.nist.gov/csrc/media/Presentations/2023/update-on-cvss-4-0/jan-25-2023-ssca-dugal-rich.pdf)). Overall, a higher base score indicates greater intrinsic severity of the vulnerability (unverified web source (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln-metrics/cvss)).

output_text: STIX 2.1 describes a standardized, machine‑readable language and serialization format for threat intelligence sharing. It defines a formal data model of interoperable object types that can be composed into a bundle to express indicators, relationships, and context for cyber threats. Core concepts include: - Objects such as Indicator, Attack Pattern, Intrusion Set, Malware, Tool, Campaign, Observed Data, Identity, Marking Definition, and Relationship; - A Bundle containing an array of objects, each with fields like id, type, created, modified, and spec_version; - A Pattern language used inside Indicator objects to describe observable indicators; - Observed Data objects to record real-world events; - Relationship objects to link objects (e.g., a malware instance uses a technique, a campaign attributed to an identity); - Data Marking and Granular Markings to control how information is shared; - Extensibility and mappings to other taxonomies such as MITRE ATT&CK. (unverified web source https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2022-12/stix-bp-v1.0.0.pdf)

answer.answer: STIX 2.1 describes a standardized, machine‑readable language and serialization format for threat intelligence sharing. It defines a formal data model of interoperable object types that can be composed into a bundle to express indicators, relationships, and context for cyber threats. Core concepts include: - Objects such as Indicator, Attack Pattern, Intrusion Set, Malware, Tool, Campaign, Observed Data, Identity, Marking Definition, and Relationship; - A Bundle containing an array of objects, each with fields like id, type, created, modified, and spec_version; - A Pattern language used inside Indicator objects to describe observable indicators; - Observed Data objects to record real-world events; - Relationship objects to link objects (e.g., a malware instance uses a technique, a campaign attributed to an identity); - Data Marking and Granular Markings to control how information is shared; - Extensibility and mappings to other taxonomies such as MITRE ATT&CK. (unverified web source https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2022-12/stix-bp-v1.0.0.pdf)

output_text:
DNS over HTTPS (DoH) reduces a SOC’s DNS visibility because it encapsulates DNS queries inside TLS-encrypted HTTPS traffic, causing domain-resolution requests to blend with normal web traffic and escape traditional DNS monitoring. This makes passive visibility of which domains endpoints are querying harder and can obscure DNS-based detections or DNS-driven data exfiltration and C2. Defenders address this challenge with a mix of strategy, telemetry, and detection logic rather than relying solely on classic DNS port 53 visibility. Key concepts and detection logic include:

- DoH encrypts DNS queries and responses, providing confidentiality and integrity and making traffic analysis less effective. This means queries are harder to distinguish from regular HTTPS traffic, reducing the ability to fingerprint or block domains based solely on DNS patterns. (unverified web source https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/networking/dns/dns-encryption-dns-over-https)

- DoH can be constrained or controlled at the network edge by enforcing enterprise resolvers or protective DNS (PDNS) to ensure visibility and policy enforcement, or by blocking non-enterprise DoH providers when break-and-inspect is not available. This aligns with guidance that organizations may block or filter DoH traffic to protect visibility. (unverified web source https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2024-05/Encrypted%20DNS%20Implementation%20Guidance_508c.pdf)

- Protective DNS capabilities and telemetry help maintain visibility by resolving queries through trusted resolvers and collecting domain-level telemetry to detect suspicious activity and outbound C2. (unverified web source https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/services/technical-reference-architecture-tra)

- Host-level DNS logging and full visibility of DNS activity remain important because many malware families rely on domain-based C2; collecting DNS data at the endpoint or through centralized resolvers preserves visibility even when DoH is used. (unverified web source https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/targeted-cyber-intrusion-detection-and-mitigation-strategies-update-b)

- DoH detection and response can leverage MITRE ATT&CK concepts for DNS (Application Layer Protocol: DNS, T1071.004) and associated detection logic, such as identifying high-volume DNS requests, encoded payload patterns, long subdomain lengths, or requests to known malicious infrastructure, which can indicate DNS-based C2 or data exfiltration even when DoH is used. (unverified web source https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/004)

- Network defenders should be aware of DoH’s impact on visibility and use a layered approach: centralize DNS enforcement through enterprise resolvers, deploy protective DNS with telemetry, enable host-level DNS logging, and apply TLS-inspection where policy and privacy allow. This comprehensive approach aligns with guidance on enhanced visibility and hardening, and with best-practice recommendations for DNS monitoring and detection. (unverified web source https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/enhanced-visibility-and-hardening-guidance-communications-infrastructure)

In short, the DoH visibility challenge is a matter of encryption and traffic pattern masking; defenders respond with policy controls, telemetry-rich DNS architectures, and detection logic aligned to DNS-centric MITRE techniques. (unverified web source https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2024-05/Encrypted%20DNS%20Implementation%20Guidance_508c.pdf, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/networking/dns/dns-encryption-dns-over-https, https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/services/technical-reference-architecture-tra, https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/004, https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/enhanced-visibility-and-hardening-guidance-communications-infrastructure, https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/targeted-cyber-intrusion-detection-and-mitigation-strategies-update-b)

Overview:
- EDR stands for Endpoint Detection and Response. It is focused on detecting, investigating, and responding to threats at the endpoint level (the device). It can block or remediate malicious activity on that single device when detections occur. [unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode)]
- XDR stands for Extended Detection and Response. It aims to unify and coordinate detection, investigation, and response across multiple security domains (endpoints, identities, email, apps, and sometimes networks) to provide a broader, enterprise-wide view and automated cross-domain response. [unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/microsoft-365-defender)]

Key differences (conceptual):
- Scope: EDR is endpoint-focused; XDR covers multiple domains across the enterprise. [unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-in-block-mode)]
- Data sources: EDR primarily ingests endpoint telemetry and behavioral signals; XDR aggregates data from endpoints plus other domains (identity, email, apps, network, cloud). [unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/microsoft-365-defender)]
- Correlation and analytics: EDR analyzes signals within the endpoint context; XDR uses cross-domain correlation to stitch together signals into broader attack stories or incidents. [unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/incidents-overview)]
- Incidents and response: EDR typically yields endpoint-focused detections and responses; XDR provides unified incidents and automated workflows across domains, often with a single pane of glass. [unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/microsoft-365-defender)]

Notes:
- In practice, many XDR offerings include EDR as the endpoint data source, making EDR a core component within an XDR solution. [unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/microsoft-365-defender)]
- Some descriptions frame XDR as an integrated layer that can ingest data beyond a single vendor’s EDR, sometimes via SIEM or other data sources to form holistic incidents. [unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security/zero-trust/siem-xdr-overview)]

Bottom line: EDR = endpoint-centric detection and response; XDR = cross-domain, enterprise-wide detection and response that aggregates and correlates signals from multiple security domains to drive broader incident management. [unverified web source (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/microsoft-365-defender)]
